real_s3.explanation: The unit responds to frontal, centered, single animal faces with both eyes visible, mainly dog faces, and extends more weakly to other furry mammal faces such as the lesser panda and probably foxes and wolves.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to frontal, centered, single animal faces with both eyes visible, mainly dog faces, and extends more weakly to other furry mammal faces such as the lesser panda and probably foxes and wolves.
parsed.evidence: Within-class activity is driven by facing the camera (frontal d +0.81, side profile -1.23, left-facing -1.35), both eyes visible (+0.84 vs one eye -0.86), and a centered subject (+0.85, 99th percentile), while the mere presence of a dog adds almost nothing (d +0.02). Non-canine furry faces such as the lesser panda score positively (+0.50).
parsed.missing_data: Activations on frontal faces of non-canine mammals such as cats and bears, and on frontal human faces, compared with dog faces, to tell whether the unit is specific to dogs or responds to frontal eye configurations in general.

real_s2.explanation: Responds to frontal, centered canine faces with both eyes clearly visible, i.e. a dog looking straight at the camera, and extends weakly to other frontal furry mammal faces (e.g., lesser panda, cats).

parsed.explanation: Responds to frontal, centered canine faces with both eyes clearly visible, i.e. a dog looking straight at the camera, and extends weakly to other frontal furry mammal faces (e.g., lesser panda, cats).
parsed.evidence: Within classes, the strongest effects are frontal orientation (d +0.81, pct 98), both eyes visible (d +0.84, pct 97), subject facing the camera (d +0.91, pct 97) and centered (d +0.85, pct 99), while profile and three-quarter views are strongly negative; simple canine presence barely matters (d +0.02), and non-canine furry faces are still positive (d +0.50, pct 94).
parsed.missing_data: Activations on frontal faces of non-canine animals and humans, plus controlled tests that vary dog head pose and position, would show whether the unit codes 'frontal mammal face with two eyes' rather than dog specifically.

parsed.evidence: The top classes are mostly dog breeds plus lesser panda. parsed.explanation: The unit responds to dogs (across many breeds) and extends weakly to similar-looking furry animals such as the lesser panda. Within those classes it prefers a whole, moderately sized animal turned toward the right (three-quarter or side view) rather than a frontal close-up of the face.

null_s3.explanation: The unit responds mainly to dogs across many breeds, with weaker extension to similar furry mammals such as the lesser panda. Within those classes it favors whole, uncropped animals turned sideways, especially facing right, not frontal eye-region close-ups.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds mainly to dogs across many breeds, with weaker extension to similar furry mammals such as the lesser panda. Within those classes it favors whole, uncropped animals turned sideways, especially facing right, not frontal eye-region close-ups.
parsed.evidence: The top classes are almost all dog breeds plus lesser panda. Within classes, the face-specific questions barely separate activity (eye-region visibility is at percentile 1, upright face at 4), frontal faces are slightly negative (d -0.22), and the strongest effects are facing right (d +0.68, percentile 98), facing toward or away from the camera (d -0.36), being fully inside the frame (d +0.32) and being cropped close-ups (d -0.21/-0.22).
parsed.missing_data: Activations on wild canids, other furry mammals and non-animal classes, plus mirrored versions of the same photos, would show whether it is dog-specific and whether the right-facing preference is real.
